en.title: Origins and early history of English
en.summary: How English grew from a Germanic language to a mixture of Old English, Norse and French.

sections.title: About this lesson
paragraphs: English is a Germanic language, related to Dutch, German and Frisian. Its words, however, come from many sources, because the history of Britain is a history of arrivals. In this lesson you will follow the story of the language from the fifth century to the age of Shakespeare. You will also learn how to tell a story in the past.

sections.title: In context
paragraphs: When the Romans left Britain in the early fifth century, groups called the Angles, the Saxons and the Jutes crossed the North Sea and settled in the land. Their speech became Old English. In 793 the Vikings attacked a monastery on the island of Lindisfarne, and over the next hundred years they settled in the north and east. By the time the Normans arrived in 1066, many Norse words had entered the language. After the Normans conquered England, French became the language of the court and the law, but ordinary people kept speaking English. While the rich spoke French, the poor were still using English words for the animals in the fields. Later, the animals on the table got French names.

| Years | Event | What happened to the language |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 5th century | Angles, Saxons and Jutes arrive from northern Europe | Old English begins |
| 793 onwards | Viking raids and settlement | Norse words enter, such as sky, egg and they |
| 1066 | The Norman Conquest | thousands of French words enter English |
| late 1300s | Chaucer writes the Canterbury Tales | London English becomes a model for writers |
| 1476 | William Caxton sets up the first printing press in England | spelling slowly becomes fixed |
| 1564 to 1616 | The life of Shakespeare | many new words and expressions appear |
| 1755 | Samuel Johnson publishes his Dictionary | it helps to fix spelling |

sections.title: Grammar notes
paragraphs: **1. Three tenses for telling a story.** Use the past simple for the main events: the Vikings attacked. Use the past continuous for what was going on in the background: while the rich spoke French, the poor were using English. Use the past perfect for something that happened earlier than the main events: by 1066 many Norse words had entered the language. See Introduction to Grammar: Past tenses and aspect.

| Tense | Form | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| past simple | base form + ed, or irregular | **The Vikings attacked.** |
| past continuous | was or were + ing | **The poor were using English.** |
| past perfect | had + past participle | **Many Norse words had entered the language.** |

**2. The passive in the past.** History often says what was done and not who did it: the word was brought, the printing press was set up. The form is was or were and the past participle. Add by when the doer matters, as in **The Canterbury Tales was written by Chaucer.** See Introduction to Grammar: Voice, reflexive and impersonal verbs.

**3. Time words link events.** Words such as when, after, before, while and by the time join two clauses and put them in order. The clause with the time word can come first or second, and a comma follows it when it comes first: **After the Normans conquered England, French became the language of the court.** See Introduction to Grammar: Conjunctions and linking clauses.

sections.title: Notice
paragraphs: The layers of history are still in the words you use. Everyday words are often older, and words for law, art or food are often French or Latin.

- **From Old English:** water, house, mother, bread, eat.
- **From Norse:** sky, egg, window, they, take.
- **From French:** justice, court, beef, pork, mutton.
- **The farm and the table:** cow, pig and sheep are old English words, and beef, pork and mutton are French words for the same animals as food.

sections.title: Culture note
paragraphs: Old English looks like a foreign language. It used letters that we no longer use, such as one called thorn, and many of its words do not look like their modern forms. The long poem Beowulf, written in Old English, is one of the most famous works in Old English.
